title: Macbeth: Banquo, Macduff, Duncan and the witches
specPoints: AO1: characters; AO2: foils and methods of characterisation

tips.title: Four measures
tips.body: Duncan measures kingship, Banquo temptation, Macduff manhood, Malcolm the king-becoming graces. Each shows what Macbeth might have been.

tips.title: Banquo is not spotless
tips.body: He resists the thought of murder but keeps silent about his suspicion in Act 3, hoping the witches may be his oracles as well.

tips.title: Macduff's answer
tips.body: I must also feel it as a man. It answers Lady Macbeth's When you durst do it, then you were a man.

tips.title: The witches never command
tips.body: They foretell and mislead; they cannot sink the sailor's ship. If you blame them, say how far, and use Banquo as the test.

why.matters: The exam can print a scene with any of these characters, and even a question about Macbeth is answered better with them in view. Foils are one of Shakespeare's most useful methods: a character placed beside another so that the difference shows. Learning Duncan, Banquo, Macduff and the witches as measures of Macbeth turns a list of people into an argument, and it gives every answer a way to move out of an extract to the play as a whole.

examples.title: The friend who took the other road
examples.body: Stories often pair two people given the same chance: two friends offered the same shortcut, one who takes it and one who does not. The second exists to show that the first had a choice. Banquo is that friend, and Macbeth is judged by him.

examples.title: Two ideas of what a man is
examples.body: Arguments about whether strength means never showing feeling are as old as this play. Lady Macbeth says a man is one who dares; Macduff says a man must also feel. The play lets both be heard, then shows which kind of man ends the tyranny.

steps.title: Duncan: the good king
steps.body:
Duncan is on stage for only a few scenes, and his job in the play is to be the king Macbeth should have served. He is generous, grateful and trusting, and the play's language gathers round him in images of growth, light and heaven.

**Trust, and its irony.** Just after the traitor Cawdor is executed, Duncan says “There’s no art To find the mind’s construction in the face” (Duncan, 1.4): “He was a gentleman on whom I built An absolute trust”. At that moment Macbeth enters. The audience, who have heard Macbeth's asides, know that Duncan is about to trust the next traitor absolutely.

**Growth.** He greets Macbeth with “I have begun to plant thee, and will labour To make thee full of growing” (Duncan, 1.4). Banquo answers in the same image: “There if I grow, The harvest is your own” (Banquo, 1.4). Macbeth answers with nothing of the kind.

**The guest.** Arriving at Inverness, Duncan says “This castle hath a pleasant seat” (Duncan, 1.6). It is the castle where he will be killed that night. After his death Macbeth envies him: “Duncan is in his grave; After life’s fitful fever he sleeps well” (Macbeth, 3.2).

rows: There's no art to find the mind's construction in the face
I have begun to plant thee
This castle hath a pleasant seat
Irony: the place of his murder
After life's fitful fever he sleeps well
props.title: Duncan in four lines

visuals.alt: A table of four lines about Duncan with what each does in the play

check.prompt: Duncan says there is no art to find the mind's construction in the face just before Macbeth enters. What is the effect?
check.solution: Duncan is speaking of the executed Cawdor, whom he trusted absolutely. Macbeth enters, and the audience, which has heard his asides about the horrid image, watches the king trust the next traitor. Shakespeare uses the audience's knowledge to make the line mean twice.

markScheme.description: Dramatic irony: the audience knows Macbeth is thinking of murder while the king speaks of trust

options: It has no effect, because Macbeth has not yet had any thought of murder
Dramatic irony: the audience knows Macbeth is thinking of murder while the king speaks of trust
It shows that Duncan has already guessed Macbeth is dangerous and is warning Banquo to watch him closely while they stay at Inverness, which is why he brings his sons with him
It proves that Duncan is a poor judge of character in every part of the play

steps.title: Banquo: the same promise, a different man
steps.body:
Banquo hears the witches at the same moment as Macbeth and is given a promise of his own: he will not be king, but his descendants will. The play uses him as a **foil**, a character whose likeness to the hero shows up the difference.

**He sees the danger.** He notices Macbeth's fear at once, “why do you start and seem to fear Things that do sound so fair?” (Banquo, 1.3), and warns him: “The instruments of darkness tell us truths” (Banquo, 1.3) to win us to our harm.

**He resists the thought.** The night of the murder he cannot sleep and prays: “Restrain in me the cursed thoughts that nature Gives way to in repose” (Banquo, 2.1). He tells Macbeth “I dreamt last night of the three Weird Sisters” (Banquo, 2.1); Macbeth claims he thinks not of them.

**But he stays silent.** In Act 3 he suspects the truth, “Thou hast it now, King, Cawdor, Glamis, all” (Banquo, 3.1), and hopes for his own line: “May they not be my oracles as well” (Banquo, 3.1). He tells no one. Macbeth fears him, “Our fears in Banquo Stick deep” (Macbeth, 3.1), and has him killed. His ghost returns to sit in Macbeth's seat.

visuals.alt: A table comparing Macbeth and Banquo as foils: their promises, first responses, the night of the murder, and Act 3

check.prompt: Why is Banquo called a foil to Macbeth?
check.solution: A foil is a character placed beside another so that the difference shows. Banquo is a soldier, hears the witches, is given a promise, and is tempted too, but prays against the cursed thoughts. The witches spoke to both; only one of them murdered. Macduff kills Macbeth, not Banquo.

markScheme.description: He gets a promise from the witches too, but resists the thought of acting on it, which shows up Macbeth's choice

options: Because he is the character who defeats Macbeth at the end of the play, as a foil in fencing is the sword that wins the match, which is why Fleance must escape
Because he is more ambitious than Macbeth
He gets a promise from the witches too, but resists the thought of acting on it, which shows up Macbeth's choice
Because he works with Macbeth to kill Duncan

steps.title: Macduff: the man who feels it as a man
steps.body:
**He finds the body.** Macduff discovers Duncan's murder and cannot name it: “O horror, horror, horror” (Macduff, 2.3); “Confusion now hath made his masterpiece” (Macduff, 2.3). When the lords go to Scone to see Macbeth crowned, he goes home instead: “No, cousin, I’ll to Fife” (Macduff, 2.4). The refusal is his first act against the new king.

**He leaves his family.** He flees to England to join Malcolm. His wife, abandoned, calls it madness: “Wisdom! to leave his wife, to leave his babes” (Lady Macduff, 4.2); “He loves us not” (Lady Macduff, 4.2). Macbeth's murderers kill her and her children.

**In England.** Malcolm tests him by pretending to be worse than Macbeth, lacking “the king-becoming graces”, and Macduff despairs for his country: “Bleed, bleed, poor country” (Macduff, 4.3); “Fit to govern? No, not to live” (Macduff, 4.3). Then Ross brings the news of his family. “All my pretty ones” (Macduff, 4.3). Malcolm tells him “Dispute it like a man” (Malcolm, 4.3); Macduff answers “I must also feel it as a man” (Macduff, 4.3).

**At the end.** He finds Macbeth, “Turn, hell-hound, turn” (Macduff, 5.8), tells him he was “from his mother’s womb Untimely ripp’d”, and kills him.

visuals.alt: A flow chart of Macduff's path: he finds Duncan's body, refuses to go to Scone, flees to England, his family is murdered, he feels it as a man, and he kills Macbeth

check.prompt: What does Macduff's reply, I must also feel it as a man, add to the play's argument about manhood?
check.solution: Malcolm tells him to take the news like a man, meaning with revenge. Macduff agrees and adds that a man must also feel it. The play has been arguing about what a man is since Act 1 Scene 7; Macduff's line gives the answer Lady Macbeth's definition left out.

markScheme.description: A man grieves as well as fights, which answers Lady Macbeth's claim that a man is one who dares to kill

options: It shows that Macduff blames himself for nothing
It shows that Macduff is weaker than Macbeth and will lose the battle, because a real soldier must never show any feeling in front of his commander, as Malcolm reminds him
It means Macduff refuses to fight Macbeth
A man grieves as well as fights, which answers Lady Macbeth's claim that a man is one who dares to kill

steps.title: The witches: what they do and what they cannot
steps.body:
The play opens on them: “When shall we three meet again” (the First Witch, 1.1); “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” (the witches, 1.1); “Hover through the fog and filthy air” (the witches, 1.1). They call themselves “The Weird Sisters, hand in hand”, and *weird* comes from the Old English *wyrd*, fate.

**They speak differently.** Most of the play is in blank verse; the witches chant in short rhyming lines with four stresses, a falling rhythm that sounds like a spell. In Act 4 they make the charm over the cauldron: “Double, double, toil and trouble” (the witches, 4.1); “Eye of newt, and toe of frog”.

**Their power has limits.** In Act 1 Scene 3 one witch plans revenge on a sailor's wife. She will “I will drain him dry as hay”, but she cannot kill him: “Though his bark cannot be lost, Yet it shall be tempest-tost” (the First Witch, 1.3). They can torment, not destroy.

**They never command.** The witches tell Macbeth what will be, never what to do. Every murder is his choice, and Banquo, who heard the same voices, made the other one. What the witches supply is truth that misleads: none of woman born, Birnam Wood.

boxes.title: What they cannot
boxes.body: Kill the sailor; make Macbeth act

visuals.alt: Four boxes on the witches: what they are, how they speak, what they can do, and what they cannot

check.prompt: What does the witch's curse on the sailor, Though his bark cannot be lost, yet it shall be tempest-tost, show about their power?
check.solution: She can keep him awake and toss his ship about, but his bark cannot be lost. Placed just before Macbeth enters, the limit on their power frames what follows: they can unsettle him, and the rest is up to him.

markScheme.description: They can torment a man but cannot destroy him, which suggests Macbeth's ruin needs his own choices

options: They can torment a man but cannot destroy him, which suggests Macbeth's ruin needs his own choices
That they are kind to sailors
That the sailor is Macbeth in disguise
That they control the weather completely and can sink any ship they choose, which is why the sailor dies before he can return to his wife, and why Macbeth fears them

steps.title: Foils: how the other characters measure Macbeth
steps.body: The supporting characters are there partly to measure the hero. Each one does something Macbeth could have done, and did not.

visuals.problem: Show how Duncan, Banquo and Macduff each act as a measure of Macbeth.

steps.text: Duncan is the king Macbeth should serve: “I have begun to plant thee, and will labour To make thee full of growing”. Kingship in him is care.
steps.note: Macbeth's kingship is fear; the contrast is the play's picture of a tyrant.

steps.text: Banquo hears the same prophecy and prays against it: “Restrain in me the cursed thoughts that nature Gives way to in repose”.
steps.note: Temptation is shown to be resistible, so Macbeth is responsible.

steps.text: Macduff grieves and acts: “I must also feel it as a man”.
steps.note: A second definition of manhood, beside Lady Macbeth's.

steps.text: Malcolm lists “the king-becoming graces”, and Macbeth has none of them.
steps.note: The play names the virtues of a king so the audience can see their absence.

steps.text: The murderer of all of them, or their families, is the one man in Scotland who has the audience's attention throughout.
steps.note: The foils make the tragedy: we see what Macbeth might have been.

visuals.alt: A table of four foils and what each measures in Macbeth: Duncan kingship, Banquo temptation, Macduff manhood, Malcolm the virtues of a king

check.prompt: Why is Banquo's prayer against the cursed thoughts that nature gives way to in repose useful in an answer about Macbeth's guilt?
check.solution: Banquo is tempted by the same promise and prays for help against it. Set beside Macbeth's dagger speech that same night, it shows two men with the same temptation and different choices, which makes Macbeth answerable for his.

markScheme.description: It shows the temptation was resistible: Banquo felt it too and fought it, so Macbeth chose

options: It shows that the witches only spoke to Banquo
It shows the temptation was resistible: Banquo felt it too and fought it, so Macbeth chose
It proves that Banquo could not sleep because of the storm
It proves that Banquo was the real murderer and Macbeth was innocent, because only a guilty man would need to pray against his thoughts on the night of a murder

steps.title: Lady Macduff and her son: the cost made visible
steps.body:
Act 4 Scene 2 is the only scene in which we meet Macduff's family, and it exists to be destroyed. Lady Macduff is angry at her husband's flight, “Wisdom! to leave his wife, to leave his babes”, and tells her son his father is dead; the boy answers her with a child's quick jokes. A messenger warns her to flee. Murderers enter, and the son is killed on stage defending his father's name.

**Why show it?** The murder of Duncan happens off stage; this one does not. Shakespeare shows the audience a home, a mother and a child, and then shows them killed for no reason but fear. It is the lowest point of Macbeth's fall, and it gives Macduff's revenge its force.

**A mirror.** Lady Macbeth imagined killing her own baby as a way to prove a promise binding. Here a real child is killed by her husband's men. The play turns her image into a fact.

visuals.alt: A table comparing Lady Macbeth and Lady Macduff: their husbands, their children, and their ends

check.prompt: Why does Shakespeare show the murder of Macduff's son on stage when he kept Duncan's off stage?
check.solution: Duncan's murder is kept in Macbeth's mind. The son's is shown in front of the audience, in a domestic scene, with no purpose behind it. The contrast measures how far Macbeth has fallen: from a murder he agonised over to one he does not even witness.

markScheme.description: To show the cost of tyranny in a home and a child, with no motive but fear

options: Because the actor playing the son was needed in the next scene
To make the audience laugh at the son's jokes
To show the cost of tyranny in a home and a child, with no motive but fear
Because the murder of a child was less shocking than the murder of a king to a Jacobean audience, so it could be shown safely without offending the Master of the Revels

steps.title: Plan an answer on Macduff
steps.body:
Take a question in the exam's shape: *Starting with Act 4 Scene 3, explore how Shakespeare presents Macduff as a hero.* Plan it in five lines.

1. The idea: what kind of hero Macduff is, and what he answers in the play.
2. Two methods in the scene: his despair for Scotland, his response to the news.
3. One moment before: the discovery of Duncan, or the refusal to go to Scone.
4. One moment after: the last fight, and untimely ripp'd.
5. One way to test the heroism: Lady Macduff's charge that he left his family.

Then write the paragraph on feel it as a man.

boxes.body: A hero who grieves as well as fights

boxes.title: In the scene
boxes.body: Bleed, bleed, poor country; All my pretty ones

visuals.alt: Four boxes planning an answer on Macduff as a hero: the idea, the scene, before and after, and the test

check.prompt: Where does Macduff go instead of to Scone to see Macbeth crowned?
check.solution: Fife, his own home: No, cousin, I'll to Fife. It is the first sign that he does not accept the new king, and it is why Macbeth later turns on him and his family.

markScheme.description: Fife

steps.title: Interpretations: do the witches cause the tragedy?
steps.body:
The question every answer on the witches meets is whether they make Macbeth murder or only reveal what was in him. The play supports both readings, and a top-level answer says so.

**For their power.** They open the play; they know he will be Cawdor before he does; their words come true; Macbeth's first line echoes theirs, “So foul and fair a day I have not seen”, as if they were already in his head.

**For his choice.** They never tell him to kill. The horrid image is his. Banquo hears the same and resists. The witch who curses the sailor cannot sink his ship. Banquo names what they do: “The instruments of darkness tell us truths” to win us to our harm.

**Context.** The play was written early in the reign of James I, who had published a book on witchcraft, *Daemonologie*, in 1597, and whose parliament passed a harsher Witchcraft Act in 1604. For that audience the witches were real and dangerous; that does not settle whether they caused the murders.

**How to write it.** *The witches supply the words and Macbeth supplies the meaning: they say king, he hears murder.*

boxes.title: Cause
boxes.body: They open the play; their words come true

boxes.title: Echo
boxes.body: So foul and fair: already in his head

boxes.title: Reveal
boxes.body: They never command; the image is his

boxes.title: Test
boxes.body: Banquo hears the same and resists

visuals.alt: Four boxes on whether the witches cause the tragedy: the case for their power, the echo, the case for his choice, and the test of Banquo

check.prompt: Which sentence explores the witches' role in the way the top level rewards?
check.solution: The top level asks for a conceptualised response that explores interpretations. The sentence about words and meaning holds both readings in one idea and points to Banquo as the test. The others assert one reading, dismiss the question, or give context with no link.

markScheme.description: The witches say king and Macbeth hears murder: they supply the words, and the meaning is his, as Banquo shows

options: In Shakespeare's time everyone believed in witches
The witches are evil and they make Macbeth kill Duncan, because they tell him that he will be king and he has no choice but to believe them and do what they say, so they are to blame
The witches are just a plot device
The witches say king and Macbeth hears murder: they supply the words, and the meaning is his, as Banquo shows

steps.title: The other characters in one page
steps.body:
Each of them measures Macbeth.

- **Duncan:** the good king; no art to find the mind's construction in the face; I have begun to plant thee; a pleasant seat.
- **Banquo:** the foil; the same promise resisted; the instruments of darkness; suspects and stays silent; killed, Fleance escapes; the ghost.
- **Macduff:** finds the body; to Fife; leaves his family; Bleed, bleed, poor country; I must also feel it as a man; untimely ripp'd.
- **Lady Macduff and her son:** a home destroyed on stage for no reason but fear.
- **The witches:** wyrd, fate; the rhyming chant; power to torment, not destroy; they never command.
- **Malcolm:** tests Macduff; names the king-becoming graces; gives the verdict.

visuals.alt: A summary table of four characters and how each measures Macbeth

check.prompt: What name do the witches call themselves, from an Old English word for fate?
check.solution: The Weird Sisters. Weird comes from the Old English wyrd, fate, so the name says what they claim to know rather than how strange they look.

markScheme.description: Weird Sisters

questions.prompt: What do the witches promise Banquo?
questions.solution: Lesser than Macbeth, and greater; thou shalt get kings, though thou be none. It is the promise that makes Macbeth kill him, and the reason the escape of Fleance matters.

markScheme.description: That his descendants will be kings, though he will not be

options: That he will be king after Macbeth, and that he will rule Scotland for many years after defeating the Norwegian army at the head of the king's forces
That he will be Thane of Cawdor
That his descendants will be kings, though he will not be
That no man of woman born can harm him

questions.prompt: Who discovers the body of Duncan?
questions.solution: Macduff, who comes early to wake the king. His horror, O horror, horror, horror, is the first honest response to the murder, and it marks him as the man who will end Macbeth.

markScheme.description: Macduff

questions.prompt: Why does Macbeth have Banquo killed?
questions.solution: Our fears in Banquo stick deep, and the crown on Macbeth's head is fruitless if Banquo's line inherits it. Banquo has in fact told no one what he suspects; the murder is driven by fear and by the prophecy.

markScheme.description: He fears Banquo, and the witches promised the crown to Banquo's descendants

options: Banquo has asked to be made king
Banquo has told Macduff about the witches and the letter, and the two of them are planning to raise an army in England with Malcolm, which Macbeth learns from his spies
Banquo has insulted Lady Macbeth at the banquet
He fears Banquo, and the witches promised the crown to Banquo's descendants

questions.prompt: What does Lady Macduff say about her husband's flight to England?
questions.solution: Wisdom! to leave his wife, to leave his babes; He loves us not. Her anger is the test of Macduff's heroism: he chose his country over his family, and the play lets his wife say what that costs.

markScheme.description: She calls it madness, not wisdom, and says he loves us not

options: She calls it madness, not wisdom, and says he loves us not
She says she told him to go
She praises his courage and tells her son that his father has gone to save Scotland from the tyrant, and that they must be proud of him and wait patiently for his return
She says nothing; she does not know he has gone

questions.prompt: Put these moments in Macduff's story in the order the play presents them.
questions.solution: Act 2 Scene 3, Act 2 Scene 4, before Act 4 Scene 2, Act 4 Scene 3, Act 5. His story runs alongside Macbeth's and ends it.

markScheme.description: the five moments in order

items: He refuses to go to Scone
He hears his family has been murdered

questions.prompt: How does Malcolm test Macduff in Act 4 Scene 3?
questions.solution: Malcolm claims to be lustful, greedy and without any of the king-becoming graces. When Macduff despairs, Fit to govern? No, not to live, Malcolm knows he is honest and takes it all back. The test shows how Macbeth's reign has taught everyone to suspect everyone.

markScheme.description: He pretends to be worse than Macbeth, to see whether Macduff is Macbeth's spy

options: He challenges him to a duel
He pretends to be worse than Macbeth, to see whether Macduff is Macbeth's spy
He sends him back to Scotland alone
He offers Macduff the crown and the throne of Scotland, to see whether he wants it for himself, and refuses to trust him when Macduff seems tempted to accept the offer

questions.prompt: Which character's son escapes when his father is murdered?
questions.solution: Banquo's son, Fleance. His father's last words, Fly, good Fleance, fly, save him, and with him the witches' promise of kings.

markScheme.description: Banquo

questions.prompt: What is unusual about how the witches speak?
questions.solution: Double, double, toil and trouble; Fire burn, and cauldron bubble: short, rhymed, four-stress lines with a falling rhythm. The difference from blank verse marks them as other, and makes their words sound like spells.

markScheme.description: Short rhyming lines with four stresses, like a chant or spell, unlike the blank verse of most characters

options: They speak only in Latin
They never speak; they only act
Short rhyming lines with four stresses, like a chant or spell, unlike the blank verse of most characters
They speak in prose throughout, like the Porter and the other comic characters, which shows the audience that they are low-born and not to be taken seriously

questions.prompt: Duncan tells Macbeth I have begun to plant thee, and will labour to make thee full of growing. Banquo answers There if I grow, the harvest is your own. What do the lines suggest?
questions.solution: Duncan speaks of planting and growth; Banquo answers in the same image, promising the harvest to the king. Macbeth says nothing of the kind, and soon asks the stars to hide their fires. The images mark who is loyal.

markScheme.description: Kingship as a gardener's care, answered with loyalty by Banquo and not by Macbeth

options: That Duncan is going to give Macbeth and Banquo land to farm as a reward for the battle, and that Banquo would rather be a farmer than a soldier, while Macbeth wants to stay in the army
That Duncan is a poor king who talks of plants instead of war
That Banquo is planning to take the crown
Kingship as a gardener's care, answered with loyalty by Banquo and not by Macbeth

questions.prompt: Why is it significant that Banquo suspects Macbeth in Act 3 but says nothing?
questions.solution: He says I fear thou play'dst most foully for't, then wonders whether the witches may be his oracles as well. The man who resisted the thought of murder does not resist the hope. Shakespeare makes even the foil less than spotless.

markScheme.description: He hopes the prophecy for his own line will come true too, so his silence is a temptation he does not resist

options: He hopes the prophecy for his own line will come true too, so his silence is a temptation he does not resist
Because he has no evidence at all and does not suspect Macbeth, which is why he goes riding with Fleance without any guard and is killed in the park near the palace
Because he is afraid of Lady Macbeth
Because he has already told Macduff

questions.prompt: Weird in the Weird Sisters comes from an Old English word. What did it mean?
questions.solution: Fate: wyrd. The name claims that the sisters know, or control, what will happen. Whether they know it or cause it is the question the play leaves open.

markScheme.description: fate

questions.prompt: What does Macbeth mean when he says of Duncan, After life's fitful fever he sleeps well?
questions.solution: The murderer envies the murdered. Duncan's life was a fever, now over; Macbeth's is scorpions in the mind. The line comes in Act 3 Scene 2, when Macbeth is king and has no rest.

markScheme.description: He envies the dead king: Duncan has peace, and Macbeth, who killed him, has none

options: He thinks Duncan is still alive
He envies the dead king: Duncan has peace, and Macbeth, who killed him, has none
He is talking about Banquo
He is pleased that Duncan died peacefully in his sleep without pain, and believes that the murder was a kindness that saved the old king from a long illness he had been suffering

questions.prompt: Which statement about the witches' power is best supported by the play?
questions.solution: They never give an order. Their prophecies come true in ways that mislead, and one of them cannot sink a sailor's ship. Banquo sees them too, so they are not only in Macbeth's head.

markScheme.description: They foretell and mislead, but never command: the choices are Macbeth's

options: They have no power at all, because none of their prophecies comes true
They are figments of Macbeth's imagination, which is why no one else sees them
They foretell and mislead, but never command: the choices are Macbeth's
They control everything that happens: they order Macbeth to kill Duncan in Act 1 Scene 3, then order him to kill Banquo and Macduff's family in Act 4 Scene 1, and he obeys each time

questions.prompt: Put these lines in the order the play presents them.
questions.solution: Act 1 Scene 4, Act 1 Scene 6, Act 2 Scene 3, Act 3 Scene 1, Act 4 Scene 3. Duncan's trust, his arrival, the discovery, the next target, the cost.

markScheme.description: the five lines in order

items: There's no art to find the mind's construction in the face
This castle hath a pleasant seat
Our fears in Banquo stick deep

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Shakespeare uses Banquo as a foil to Macbeth. Refer to at least two moments and say what each shows about Macbeth.
questions.solution: Shakespeare gives Banquo the same experience as Macbeth so that the audience can see what Macbeth chose. Both hear the witches; both are promised something. Banquo's first response is to notice his friend's fear, “why do you start and seem to fear Things that do sound so fair?”, and to warn him that “The instruments of darkness tell us truths” to win us to our harm: he reads the prophecy as a danger, where Macbeth is already imagining a murder. The night of the killing, Banquo cannot sleep either, but he prays: “Restrain in me the cursed thoughts that nature Gives way to in repose”. Set beside Macbeth's dagger speech a few lines later, the prayer shows that the temptation could be resisted, and so Macbeth is answerable for yielding. Yet Shakespeare does not make the foil spotless. In Act 3 Banquo suspects the truth, “Thou hast it now, King, Cawdor, Glamis, all”, and hopes instead: “May they not be my oracles as well”. He tells no one. The man who resisted the thought of murder does not resist the hope it would profit him, and the contrast becomes more interesting than good against evil: Banquo shows how temptation works on an ordinary conscience, and Macbeth shows what happens when it is obeyed.

The man who resisted the thought of murder does not resist the hope it would profit him, and the contrast becomes more interesting than good against evil: Banquo shows how temptation works on an ordinary conscience, and Macbeth shows what happens when it is obeyed.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Shakespeare presents Macduff's idea of manhood, and how it answers Lady Macbeth's.
questions.solution: When Ross tells Macduff that his wife and children have been murdered, his first words are a father's, “All my pretty ones”, not a soldier's. Malcolm urges revenge, “Dispute it like a man”, and Macduff agrees, but adds: “I must also feel it as a man”. The line answers an argument the play began in Act 1 Scene 7, where Lady Macbeth told her husband “When you durst do it, then you were a man”, making manhood a matter of daring to kill. Macduff's manhood includes grief, and it is he, not the man who dared all, who ends the tyranny. Shakespeare does not make him perfect: his wife, abandoned, calls his flight madness, “Wisdom! to leave his wife, to leave his babes”, and says “He loves us not”, and he blames himself when he hears the news. But the contrast is the point. Macbeth's daring has made him numb, supp'd full with horrors; Macduff feels the loss and acts on it, and the play sets his definition of a man against the one that destroyed Scotland.

questions.prompt: A student writes: "The witches are to blame for everything." What is the better account?
questions.solution: The witches matter, and a good answer says how; but they never command, the horrid image is his, and Banquo is the test that shows the choice. A how-far judgement holds both.

markScheme.description: The witches tempt and mislead, but the murderous thought is his and Banquo resists the same voices

questions.prompt: Why does the play show Malcolm listing the king-becoming graces in Act 4?
questions.solution: Justice, verity, temperance, stableness, bounty, perseverance, mercy, lowliness, devotion, patience, courage, fortitude: Malcolm names twelve graces and pretends to lack them all. The list is a standard against which the tyrant is judged, and it prepares for Malcolm as the restored king.

markScheme.description: To name the virtues of a true king, so the audience can measure Macbeth's reign by their absence

options: To name the virtues of a true king, so the audience can measure Macbeth's reign by their absence
Because Malcolm wants to prove that he is a better speaker than Macduff and that he deserves the crown more than Macduff does, which is why Macduff leaves the stage in anger at the end
To delay the arrival of Ross
Because the list was required by the Master of the Revels

examTechnique.body:
**Any character can carry the extract.** Know Duncan, Banquo, Macduff, Malcolm and the witches well enough to place their scenes and quote them.

**Use foils for the whole-text move.** A question on Macbeth can move out to Banquo or Macduff: the contrast is a method, and it shows the whole play.

**On the witches, answer how far.** Their power and its limits, with Banquo as the test.

**Context in a sentence.** James I's *Daemonologie* and the 1604 Witchcraft Act explain why the witches were frightening, not that they caused anything.
examinerErrors: Saying the witches order Macbeth to kill, when they never do.
Saying Banquo kills Macbeth, or that Fleance does; Macduff does.
Treating Banquo as simply good, without his silence in Act 3.
Forgetting Lady Macduff, whose scene gives Macduff's story its cost.
Writing about the witches and the 1600s in a paragraph with no line from the play.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer uses the other characters as measures. It reads Banquo as a foil and notices where he is less than a hero; it sets Macduff's feel it as a man against Lady Macbeth's durst; it judges the witches' power with their limits and with Banquo as the test; and it ties the context of James I's court to a line rather than a paragraph. Quotations are exact and short, and each says what the contrast shows.
